title_en: The Biggest Mess Wuhan Ever Made
excerpt_en: Wuhan has had no shortage of scandals — but one answer to 'why hasn't it declined' says the biggest mess of all was the one in early 2020, and next to it, everything else barely counts.
body_en:
Wuhan has had no shortage of scandals in recent years — so why hasn't it declined?

A noodle-shop beheading, masks, false accusations, a cherry-blossom university, Halloween... one after another. Any other city might have been nailed to the pillar of shame by now. But one answer put it this way: the biggest mess Wuhan ever made was this one — and next to it, everything else barely counts.

The biggest mess: those two months in early 2020

On February 26, 2020, Caijing magazine reconstructed what happened. Before Zhong Nanshan confirmed human-to-human transmission of the coronavirus, two expert teams visited Wuhan to investigate — and came away concluding there was "no clear evidence of human-to-human transmission" and that the outbreak was "preventable and controllable."

Why that conclusion? A member of the second team said they had suspected human-to-human transmission all along, but the information and data available to them were limited — there was no evidence. Early cases were mostly linked to the Huanan seafood market, and whether that meant common exposure or transmission between people, the disease-control experts they asked could not say for sure.

The expert believed Wuhan's non-cooperation was the main problem. Everywhere they went, they asked whether any medical staff had been infected. The answer was always no. "Looking back now, they were lying."

Had they been told of even a single infected medical worker, the expert team's assessment would have been entirely different. But "if people don't tell the truth, there's nothing we can do — we were basically just there for clinical treatment."

The team also found 41 confirmed cases by testing, plus a larger batch of suspected cases. The experts agreed unanimously: report both the suspected and the confirmed. But in the end, the local authorities reported only the confirmed cases. "When we asked them to report truthfully, a Health Commission leader shot back: 'Are you suggesting I'm covering things up?' Once he said that, what more could we say?"

On February 10, Zhang Jin, the former Party secretary of the Hubei Health Commission, and Liu Yingzi, its former director, were removed from their posts.

Next to this, everything else barely counts

A noodle-shop beheading damages the reputation of a bowl of noodles. A cherry-blossom university and Halloween damage a city's image. However much they trend, they pass.

Those two months in early 2020 were different. The information never made it up, so the judgment was wrong; the judgment was wrong, and the price was not one city's to pay.

Whether a city declines is not measured by how many times it trends. It is measured by how big a mess it has made — and whether it learned anything from it. Wuhan made its biggest one six years ago.
